title: Dispensing Automation and Packaging: Dispensing Devices, Pickup Systems, Processing Automation, Compliance Packaging, Planners and Child-Resistant Containers
topic: Dispensing / Automated devices and dispensing packaging
subtopic: Automated dispensing devices under 247 CMR 9.12 with Board and Drug Control Program Policy 2019-02 and technician stocking under Policy 2023-08; patient-facing Automated Pharmacy Systems under 247 CMR 9.10 with Board Policy 2022-07; Pharmacy Processing Automation under 247 CMR 9.11; compliance packaging under 247 CMR 9.08 as republished 12/6/2024 (Mass. Register #1536), including multi-drug-single-dose return and repackaging and package labels, with Board Policy 2023-01; reusable daily dosage planners under 247 CMR 9.07; and special (child-resistant) packaging of oral prescription drugs under 15 U.S.C. 1471-1476 and 16 CFR 1700.1, 1700.14, 1700.15 and 1700.20, the prescriber's and purchaser's routes to a conventional container, CPSC staff guidance, and the absence as of 2026-09-16 of a separate Massachusetts packaging requirement in the sources searched
learning_objectives: Classify a piece of pharmacy automation as an automated dispensing device, an Automated Pharmacy System or Pharmacy Processing Automation, and apply only that device's conditions.
State the four conditions of 247 CMR 9.12 and the Policy 2019-02 requirements on ownership, licensing-body approval, access, packaging, loss reporting and two-year onsite records.
Distinguish the loader lists for a retail pharmacy's emergency-kit device and its daily-dispensing device, with the registration and video requirements of each.
Apply the Policy 2023-08 facility threshold and match each technician credential to its schedules, verification and validation conditions.
Apply the Schedule IV-VI, location, security, product, verification, record, consultation and patient-choice conditions of 247 CMR 9.10.
State the verification and comingled-lot conditions of 247 CMR 9.11.
Apply 247 CMR 9.08 to each compliance packaging type, including the multi-drug-single-dose limits, return and repackaging, and label contents.
Apply 247 CMR 9.07 to a reusable daily dosage planner and separate the regulation from Policy 2023-01's additions.
Decide when an oral prescription drug must be in special packaging, who may obtain a conventional container and how, and what CPSC staff guidance adds.
Explain how 247 CMR 9.08 and the federal special packaging requirement apply together, and what the Massachusetts search found.

orientation.text: Massachusetts regulates four different kinds of pharmacy automation, and the first question in any scenario is which one is in front of you, because the conditions do not travel from one to another. An automated dispensing device, governed by 247 CMR 9.12 and by Board and Drug Control Program Policy 2019-02, is the cabinet that Policy 2019-02 describes as designed for use in health care facilities, storing drugs and releasing them to licensed health care professionals near the point of care. An Automated Pharmacy System, governed by 247 CMR 9.10 and Board Policy 2022-07, is patient-facing: it releases a filled prescription to the patient or the patient's agent. Pharmacy Processing Automation under 247 CMR 9.11 is the equipment inside the pharmacy that counts, fills vials or compliance packaging and labels. Technician stocking of dispensing devices has its own policy, Policy 2023-08. Each of these texts speaks of controlled substances, and in Massachusetts that term is not limited to federally scheduled drugs: under 105 CMR 700.002(F) Schedule VI takes in prescription drugs not placed in Schedules I through V.

247 CMR 9.12 lets a pharmacy use an automated dispensing device for controlled substances on four conditions: the device is located in a licensed health care facility; dispensing is pursuant to a valid patient specific prescription or order; utilization is in accordance with all laws, regulations and policies; and the pharmacy maintains policies and procedures on location, operation and maintenance, security, controlled substances accountability, quality assurance, stocking and return activities, and patient confidentiality. The third condition brings Policy 2019-02 into the regulation. That policy keeps the device and its contents the property of the pharmacy until dispensed for administration; requires the facility, if it has no on-site pharmacy, to determine whether approval from its licensing body is required for the use and placement of the device; puts its own policies, procedures and quality assurance programs on the facility; restricts access to authorized licensed personnel with a periodically reviewed user list; requires medications to be in the manufacturer's sealed, original packaging or repackaged for a single dose or person; and requires losses to be reported under the requirements of the pharmacy's licensing body. The policy says dispensing must be pursuant to a valid patient-specific prescription, and the regulation says prescription or order; stock pulled against no patient-specific authorization satisfies neither.

The record set under Policy 2019-02 is kept onsite at the pharmacy, not at the facility, for not less than 2 years and readily available upon request. It includes documentation of the licensing body's approval if applicable, the locations of all devices, delivery manifests or similar electronic documentation tracking controlled substances between the pharmacy and the device, cleaning and maintenance logs, and data on every event: who accessed the contents, which system location, the type of transaction with its date and time stamp, the name, strength, dosage form and quantity of the product, the patient's name or other identifier, and reconciliation of all inventory activities. The general controlled-substance security, inventory and theft-or-loss rules that sit behind this record set are taught in the sections on controlled-substance security and on inventory and records, and the reconciliation here is in addition to them.

Policy 2019-02 then separates retail pharmacies that place devices in facilities by what the device is for. A device used for an emergency medication kit or a similar approved use, such as a Hospice Inpatient Facility, may be loaded by a Massachusetts-licensed pharmacist, pharmacy intern, certified pharmacy technician, nurse, or pharmacy technician, the last for Schedules III through VI only; a non-resident retail pharmacy needs a machine-specific Controlled Substance Registration from the Board and must determine whether a machine-specific DEA number is also required, and the same registration step applies to the device retail pharmacies must utilize for acute use medications in Hospice Inpatient Facilities. The kits and hospice supplies themselves belong to the section on supplying medication outside the pharmacy counter. A device used for daily medication dispensing is held to more: a machine-specific DEA number (if applicable) and Controlled Substance Registration, continuous video monitoring, and loading only by a Massachusetts-licensed pharmacist, or by a certified pharmacy technician or pharmacy intern while supervised by a Massachusetts licensed pharmacist. A nurse or an ordinary technician is on the first list and not on the second.

Policy 2023-08, adopted jointly by the Board, the Drug Control Program and the Bureau of Healthcare Safety and Quality on 6/1/23, lets Board-licensed technicians stock devices in patient care areas, but only inside a Massachusetts-licensed health care facility that has an on-site pharmacy and whose devices are at the same physical address as the facility's Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration. The pharmacy must determine whether the facility's licensing authority requires approvals or notices, keep policies and procedures with training requirements, and follow Policy 2019-02; a licensed health care professional must use bar code scanning or other electronic validation upon removal from the device and/or upon patient administration; and a designated Board-licensed individual verifies all transactions against what the pharmacy sent or expects back, monitors all access, tracks and trends data, and random audits are conducted. Within those walls there are three pathways. A pharmacy technician trainee may, without direct pharmacist supervision but under the direction and supervision of a pharmacist, transport and load pharmacist-verified Schedule III through VI stock and remove expired Schedule III through VI stock, using electronic validation. Every other licensed technician may do the same for Schedules II through VI, under pharmacist supervision. A nationally certified licensed technician may, without prior pharmacist verification, remove non-patient specific Schedule VI medications, excluding Prescription Monitoring Program drugs such as gabapentin, from an electronic inventory management system without further manipulation and load them into a device, using electronic validation.

Two points about that policy need care, and neither is resolved by its text. First, 247 CMR 2.00 describes technicians and trainees as working under the direct supervision of a pharmacist, and the policy expressly allows trainee stocking without direct supervision; that is a jointly issued, dated policy permission confined to its own facility, verification and validation conditions, and the general supervision rules are taught in the sections on pharmacy technicians and support personnel. Second, the policy's Schedule II pathway for licensed technicians who are not certified sits beside 247 CMR 8.05, which frames an ordinary technician's role with Schedule II stock as assisting with transport. Whether the policy enlarges that role at a hospital device is arguable. The course that is safe on either reading is to have Schedule II device loading done by a certified pharmacy technician or a pharmacist, and in every case to meet all of the policy's conditions, including pharmacist-verified stock and electronic validation.

The Automated Pharmacy System is where a patient collects a filled prescription, and 247 CMR 9.10 draws it narrowly. A pharmacy may dispense Schedule IV through VI controlled substances from it to a patient or the patient's agent during or after pharmacy hours, provided the system is within the same building as the pharmacy; is secured against or within a wall or floor; is monitored with its location by continuous, recordable video surveillance; holds nothing that requires refrigeration or reconstitution; uses industry standard technological verification to ensure the correct medication reaches the correct patient; generates an electronic audit trail that includes the identity of each person to whom a drug was released; is backed by an opportunity for pharmacist consultation during all hours the system is in operation for dispensing; and is optional for the patient. Written policies cover location, operation and maintenance, security, controlled substances accountability, quality assurance, stocking and return activities and confidentiality. Policy 2022-07, which predates the 2024 text, adds that a Board-licensed pharmacy submits a written request for Board approval before use, that an approved system is an extension of the licensed area, that the offer to counsel is provided for new or changed therapy, and that for Schedule IV, V and Schedule VI additional drugs such as gabapentin the identity of the person receiving the medication is collected, PMP reporting is met and the DEA is consulted. Where the policy words the consultation duty more narrowly than the regulation, the regulation's all-hours wording controls. The counseling duty itself is taught in the section on patient counseling.

Pharmacy Processing Automation under 247 CMR 9.11 does not dispense to anyone; it is how the pharmacy counts, fills vials or compliance packaging, and labels. It is permitted on two conditions. The automation must use a technological verification, such as bar code, electronic, weight or radio frequency identification verification or another similar process, to ensure the correct medication is dispensed. And if lot numbers are comingled in a single cell, the pharmacy must maintain a policy and procedure to quarantine all comingled lot numbers in the event a single lot number is recalled; comingling is conditioned, not forbidden. The pharmacy also implements and maintains policies and procedures on operation and maintenance, security, controlled substance accountability, quality assurance, and stocking and return activities. Off-site processing, central fill and shared services are different arrangements and are taught in the section on supplying medication outside the pharmacy counter.

Compliance packaging under 247 CMR 9.08, as republished on 12/6/2024 (Mass. Register #1536), comes in three named types: oral-liquid-single-dose, single-drug-single-dose and multi-drug-single-dose. Every type requires a designated space that prevents cross contamination; written procedures for each type on cleaning, labeling, dispensing, hand hygiene, quarantine and reverse distribution; no conflict with the USP-DI monograph or FDA-approved labeling; compatibility of the medications with the packaging components and with each other; packaging designed so the container cannot be re-closed, shows evidence of having been opened, and carries a label that cannot be altered or removed; no quantity beyond the container's capacity or that may damage the dosage forms; adherence to USP requirements for containers and packaging; and not more than one commercially available medication in an oral-liquid-single-dose package unless compounded pursuant to a prescription. Single-drug-single-dose packaging is for solid oral dosage forms, and it may be prepared before a patient specific prescription arrives, but then the pharmacy and pharmacist must properly label the package and use bar-code scanning or similar technology to identify the pre-packaged medication at the time of dispensing.

Multi-drug-single-dose packaging is also for solid oral dosage forms, and 247 CMR 9.08(3) puts three limits on it: no more than a 60-day supply, no Schedule II or III controlled substances, and no medications to be taken on an as needed basis. The Schedule II and III limit is tied to this packaging type, so the same drug may go in its own single-drug-single-dose package, and maintenance therapy is not an exception. Under 9.08(4) the pharmacy may take back a multi-drug-single-dose package it previously dispensed, remove a discontinued drug, add a new medication after a therapy change, and re-dispense to that same patient, after relabeling under 9.08(5) and under written procedures for controlled-substance security and accountability. Medication removed may not go back to inventory or to any other patient, and the pharmacy keeps a record of the repackaging, removal or re-dispensing that identifies the pharmacist making the change. The general rules on returning medication to stock and re-dispensing are taught in the section on returns, recalls and product integrity; this is the compliance-packaging carve-out.

The label on each oral-liquid-single-dose, single-drug-single-dose and multi-drug-single-dose package, under 247 CMR 9.08(5), carries the information required by M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 and USP for each medication; the name, strength, physical description and total quantity of each drug; the dispensing or preparation date; for each drug in a multi-drug-single-dose package, a beyond-use date that may not exceed the shortest expiration date on the original manufacturer's container or 60 days; and the pharmacy's telephone number. A package with removable cells has each cell labeled with each drug name and strength under 9.08(6). The statutory label itself is taught in the section on the dispensing label and record. Board Policy 2023-01, revised 1/9/25, restates these conditions and adds drug accountability to the written procedures for compliance packaging; its multi-drug-single-dose passages begin 'Unless otherwise prohibited' and do not repeat the Schedule II and III limit, which the regulation still imposes.

A reusable daily dosage planner is a different container with a different trigger. Under 247 CMR 9.07 the pharmacy may dispense into one at the patient's or the patient's agent's request, provided the pharmacy places in it no medication previously dispensed by a different pharmacy; designates a space for orderly preparation that prevents cross-contamination; keeps procedures on cleaning, labeling, dispensing and hand hygiene; cleans and stores planners so as to prevent contamination; and labels each planner with all information required by M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 for each medication. Policy 2023-01 adds, as Board policy rather than regulation, that the procedures include inspection of container integrity and drug accountability, that the medications are compatible with each other, and that no more than a 60-day supply is dispensed in a planner.

Child-resistant packaging is federal law. The Poison Prevention Packaging Act, 15 U.S.C. 1471 to 1476, and 16 CFR 1700.14(a)(10) require any human drug in a dosage form intended for oral administration that federal law restricts to prescription dispensing to be in special packaging meeting 16 CFR 1700.15, unless it is on the list of exemptions in that paragraph, each bounded by its own form, strength or package limits: sublingual nitroglycerin, sublingual and chewable isosorbide dinitrate of 10 milligrams or less, cyclically administered oral contraceptives in manufacturers' mnemonic dispenser packages, unit dose potassium supplements of not more than 50 milliequivalents per unit dose, methylprednisolone tablets in packages of not more than 84 mg, prednisone tablets in packages of no more than 105 mg, medroxyprogesterone acetate tablets and others. Special packaging means packaging significantly difficult for children under five to open or to obtain a toxic or harmful amount from within a reasonable time and not difficult for normal adults to use properly; it is not packaging no child can open. Under 16 CFR 1700.15(b) and 1700.20 it must show child-resistant effectiveness of not less than 85 percent without a demonstration and 80 percent after one, and, apart from aerosol and metal-container products, senior adult use effectiveness of not less than 90 percent, and under 1700.15(c) special packaging shall not be reused. The search of Massachusetts sources for this section found no separate state child-resistance rule for dispensed drugs: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 requires a labeled container without a child-resistance element, 247 CMR 9.00 and 105 CMR 700.000 add nothing, and 15 U.S.C. 1476(a) bars a State from keeping a non-identical special packaging standard in effect while the federal one applies, except as 1476(b) and (c) provide.

A conventional container is available by only two routes under 15 U.S.C. 1473(b): a drug dispensed on a practitioner's order may go in a noncomplying package only when directed in that order or when requested by the purchaser. The manufacturer's single-size allowance in 1473(a) is a separate provision that the pharmacist does not use. The Consumer Product Safety Commission's guide for healthcare professionals, revised 2005, is staff guidance and not regulation, and it fills in the practice. A patient may ask that all of his or her prescriptions be dispensed in non-special packaging, a blanket waiver, but a request for one prescription is not a blanket waiver; the law does not require the request to be in writing, though the staff recommends it; a prescriber's standing direction reaches only refills of the prescription that carried it; plastic vials are not to be reused for refills, while the staff has no objection to reusing a glass container with a new closure; and drugs for patients confined in a hospital, or supplied to a traditional nursing home where staff administer the doses, need not be in special packaging because the test is whether the package is likely to enter a home.

Where compliance packaging and the federal packaging rules meet, each binds on its own terms. 247 CMR 9.08 demands a non-reclosable, opening-evident package with a label that cannot be altered or removed, but it says nothing about child resistance, and the Commission's staff guidance states that a tamper-evident package is not necessarily child-resistant and that unit dose packaging such as blisters or pouches must meet the special packaging standards. A multi-drug-single-dose card of oral prescription drugs going to a patient's home therefore needs to meet 16 CFR 1700.15 unless a purchaser request or prescriber direction for noncomplying packaging is on file or every drug in it is exempt; the stricter requirements of both apply together. A reusable planner raises a harder question. The patient's request for a planner is required by 247 CMR 9.07, but neither text says whether that request is also the purchaser's request for noncomplying packaging, and a planner that is reused is not special packaging under 1700.15(c). The safe course on either reading is to record an express purchaser request for noncomplying packaging when oral prescription drugs that are not exempt are dispensed into a planner. Inside a hospital, a dispensing device releasing doses for administration to confined patients is outside the household packaging concern on the staff guidance's own test.

worked_examples.scenario: A retail pharmacy supplies a skilled nursing facility and wants one cabinet there to replace its emergency kit and a second cabinet for daily dispensing. The staffing plan has a facility nurse and the pharmacy's ordinary licensed technician load both cabinets, and the pharmacy registers only the first cabinet.
steps: Classify each cabinet by purpose under Policy 2019-02, because the loader list and registration steps follow the purpose, not the building or the owner.

For the emergency-kit cabinet, a nurse is a listed loader and an ordinary licensed pharmacy technician may load Schedules III through VI only; Schedule II stock must be loaded by a pharmacist, intern or certified technician.

For the daily-dispensing cabinet, loading is limited to a pharmacist, or a certified pharmacy technician or pharmacy intern supervised by a Massachusetts licensed pharmacist, so neither the nurse nor the ordinary technician may load it.

Add the daily-dispensing cabinet's own requirements: a machine-specific Controlled Substance Registration, a machine-specific DEA number if applicable, and continuous video monitoring, on top of the 247 CMR 9.12 conditions and the two-year onsite record set.
worked_examples.resolution: The emergency-kit plan works only if Schedule II loading is moved to an eligible loader; the daily-dispensing plan fails on its loaders, its registration and video. The error invited is carrying the broader emergency-kit loader list over to a daily-dispensing device.

worked_examples.scenario: A hospital with an on-site pharmacy uses devices in its patient care units at the address on its MCSR. A trainee loads pharmacist-verified alprazolam with bar code scanning; a licensed non-certified technician loads verified methylphenidate; a certified technician pulls sealed gabapentin from the carousel without pharmacist verification and loads it.
steps: Confirm the Policy 2023-08 threshold first: a licensed facility with an on-site pharmacy, devices at the MCSR address, written procedures with training, and the designated licensee's quality assurance duties.

The trainee's action fits: Schedule IV is within III through VI, the stock is pharmacist-verified, and electronic validation is used; the trainee remains under a pharmacist's direction and supervision.

The licensed technician's action fits the policy's Schedule II through VI pathway, but because 247 CMR 8.05 frames an ordinary technician's Schedule II role as assisting with transport, the reading is arguable and the safe course is a certified technician or pharmacist for the Schedule II load.

The certified technician's action fails: the no-prior-verification pathway is for non-patient specific Schedule VI stock excluding PMP drugs, and gabapentin is reported to the PMP under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) and the Department's data submission guide for dispensers.
worked_examples.resolution: Only the gabapentin load is outside the policy; it can be done through an ordinary verified-stock pathway instead. The error invited is treating national certification as a way around the PMP exclusion, or treating technician as one credential.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy installs a pickup kiosk in the lobby of its own building, wall-anchored and on recorded video. It plans to stock filled prescriptions for oxycodone, alprazolam and insulin glargine for after-hours pickup, with pharmacist consultation available by phone during store hours only.
steps: Identify the device as an Automated Pharmacy System under 247 CMR 9.10, because it releases filled prescriptions to patients, not an automated dispensing device.
Oxycodone is Schedule II, outside the Schedule IV through VI limit in 9.10(1).
Insulin glargine requires refrigeration, and 9.10(1)(d) bars stocking medications that require refrigeration or reconstitution.

Consultation must be available during all hours the system is in operation for dispensing under 9.10(1)(g), so store hours alone do not meet it for after-hours pickup; the patient must also be allowed to decline the kiosk, and Policy 2022-07 describes a written request for Board approval before use.
worked_examples.resolution: Only the alprazolam fits, and only once consultation covers the kiosk's dispensing hours; Board policy also expects the written approval request before use. The error invited is treating security and video as the whole test while missing the schedule, refrigeration and consultation conditions.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient's caregiver asks for a 90-day supply of the patient's scheduled morning and evening tablets in multi-drug-single-dose cards, including buprenorphine tablets taken daily, an anxiolytic the patient takes only as needed, and a Schedule IV sleep aid taken nightly, with a beyond-use date 90 days out.
steps: Apply 247 CMR 9.08(3)(a): no more than a 60-day supply may be dispensed in a multi-drug-single-dose package, so 90 days is too much.

Apply 9.08(3)(b): buprenorphine is Schedule III and may not be in a multi-drug-single-dose package, whatever its maintenance use; it may go in its own single-drug-single-dose package if the other conditions are met.
Apply 9.08(3)(c): a medication taken as needed may not be in the multi-drug-single-dose package; the Schedule IV sleep aid is not excluded by schedule.
Apply 9.08(5)(d): the beyond-use date for each drug may not exceed the shortest expiration date on the original manufacturer's container or 60 days.
worked_examples.resolution: The cards may hold up to 60 days of the scheduled non-Schedule II or III tablets with a beyond-use date no later than the shorter limit; buprenorphine goes separately and the as-needed drug stays out. The error invited is reading the Schedule II and III limit as a ban on all packaging or maintenance as an exception.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient returns a multi-drug-single-dose card the pharmacy dispensed last week because the prescriber stopped one drug and started another. A technician suggests pulling the stopped tablets back into stock and giving the unused new-drug stock to another patient's card.
steps: 247 CMR 9.08(4)(a) lets the pharmacy accept the card it previously dispensed and remove the discontinued drug, add the new medication, and re-dispense to that same patient.
The removed tablets may not be returned to inventory and may not be dispensed to any patient other than the one who returned the card under 9.08(4)(b).

Relabel under 9.08(5) before re-dispensing, follow the written procedures for controlled-substance security and accountability during return and repackaging, and record the change with the pharmacist who made it under 9.08(4)(c).
worked_examples.resolution: Repackage and re-dispense to the same patient only, quarantine the removed tablets for disposal under the pharmacy's procedures, and document the pharmacist. The error invited is treating medication removed from a returned card as ordinary return-to-stock product.

worked_examples.scenario: An older patient with arthritis asks for easy-open caps on all her prescriptions from now on. A week later a prescription arrives from a different prescriber marked for a conventional container, and her daughter, who lives with young children, picks up a refill of another prescription and asks for a child-resistant cap.
steps: Under 15 U.S.C. 1473(b) a noncomplying package is permitted only when directed in the order or requested by the purchaser; the patient's request for all prescriptions is a purchaser request, and CPSC staff guidance says a pharmacist may rely on such a blanket request, recommending it be in writing though the law does not require it.
The new prescription's marking is a prescriber direction for that prescription; on staff guidance it would also reach that prescription's refills, but not her other prescriptions.

The daughter, as purchaser, may ask for special packaging on the refill; the staff guidance treats periodic checking of blanket requests as prudent, so confirm the patient's current preference and record the change.
Use a new special-packaging container rather than a reused vial, because 16 CFR 1700.15(c) says special packaging shall not be reused.
worked_examples.resolution: Conventional caps are lawful on the patient's blanket request and on the prescriber's direction, and the refill goes in new child-resistant packaging when the purchaser asks. The error invited is treating the pharmacist's own judgment, or one request, as settling every future container.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: State the four conditions on which 247 CMR 9.12 lets a pharmacy use an automated dispensing device for controlled substances.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The device is located in a licensed health care facility; dispensing is pursuant to a valid patient specific prescription or order; utilization is in accordance with all laws, regulations and policies; and the pharmacy maintains device policies and procedures on location, operation and maintenance, security, controlled substances accountability, quality assurance, stocking and return activities, and patient confidentiality.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under Policy 2019-02, who owns a device and its contents, and until when?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The pharmacy, until the medication is dispensed for administration.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A facility without an on-site pharmacy wants a pharmacy-owned cabinet. What does Policy 2019-02 require about licensing-body approval?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The facility must determine whether approval from its licensing body is required for the use and placement of the device; if approval is obtained, documentation of it is part of the pharmacy's records.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where and for how long are Policy 2019-02 device records kept?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Onsite at the pharmacy for not less than 2 years, readily available upon request.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who may load a retail pharmacy's device used for daily medication dispensing?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A Massachusetts-licensed pharmacist, or a certified pharmacy technician or pharmacy intern while supervised by a Massachusetts licensed pharmacist.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What two facility facts must be true before any Policy 2023-08 technician stocking pathway is used?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The Massachusetts-licensed health care facility has an on-site pharmacy, and the devices are at the same physical address as listed on the facility's Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which schedules may a pharmacy technician trainee load under Policy 2023-08, and on what stock?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Schedules III through VI, pharmacist-verified stock only, using barcode scanning or other electronic validation.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which stock fits the certified technician's no-prior-verification pathway in Policy 2023-08?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Non-patient specific Schedule VI medications, excluding PMP drugs such as gabapentin, removed from an electronic inventory management system without further manipulation and loaded with electronic validation.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which schedules may be dispensed from an Automated Pharmacy System, and where must it be?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Schedules IV through VI, from a system located within the same building as the pharmacy.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What products may never be stocked in an Automated Pharmacy System?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Medications that require refrigeration or reconstitution.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: During what hours must pharmacist consultation be available for an Automated Pharmacy System?
retrieval_prompts.answer: During all hours that the system is in operation for dispensing, under 247 CMR 9.10(1)(g).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: May Pharmacy Processing Automation comingle lot numbers in one cell?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Yes, if the pharmacy maintains a policy and procedure to quarantine all comingled lot numbers in the event a single lot number is recalled.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the three limits 247 CMR 9.08(3) puts on multi-drug-single-dose packaging.
retrieval_prompts.answer: No more than a 60-day supply; no Schedule II or III controlled substances; no medications to be taken on an as needed basis.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must happen when a single-drug-single-dose package is prepared before a patient specific prescription is received?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The pharmacy and pharmacist properly label the package and use bar-code scanning or similar technology to identify the pre-packaged medication at the time of dispensing.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What beyond-use date goes on each drug in a multi-drug-single-dose package?
retrieval_prompts.answer: One that does not exceed the shortest expiration date on the original manufacturer's container or 60 days.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What design features does 247 CMR 9.08(1)(e) require of compliance packaging?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It is designed to prevent the container from being re-closed, to show evidence of having been opened, and so that the label cannot be altered or removed.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What may happen to a medication removed from a returned multi-drug-single-dose package?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It may not be returned to inventory and may not be dispensed to any patient other than the patient who returned the package.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who may start the reusable daily dosage planner service, and what product may not go into the planner?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The patient or the patient's agent, by request; no medication previously dispensed by a different pharmacy may be placed in it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where does the 60-day limit on a reusable daily dosage planner come from?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Board Policy 2023-01, not 247 CMR 9.07.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which dispensed drugs does 16 CFR 1700.14(a)(10) require to be in special packaging?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Human drugs in a dosage form intended for oral administration that federal law requires to be dispensed only on a prescription, except the listed exemptions.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who may cause a prescription drug to be dispensed in a noncomplying package under 15 U.S.C. 1473(b)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The prescriber, by directing it in the order, or the purchaser, by requesting it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: the law requires a patient's request for conventional packaging to be in writing.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. CPSC staff guidance states the law and regulations do not require a written request, though the staff recommends one, particularly for a blanket request.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: May a plastic prescription vial be reused for a refill?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. 16 CFR 1700.15(c) says special packaging shall not be reused; CPSC staff guidance separately states no objection to reusing a glass container with a new closure.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does Massachusetts law add its own child-resistant packaging requirement for dispensed drugs?
retrieval_prompts.answer: None was found as of 2026-09-16 in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21, the General Laws search, 247 CMR 9.00 or 105 CMR 700.000, and 15 U.S.C. 1476 preempts non-identical State standards except as 1476(b) and (c) provide.

quick_review.text: Identify the device first: a dispensing device serves licensed professionals in a facility, an Automated Pharmacy System serves patients picking up filled prescriptions, and Pharmacy Processing Automation fills and labels inside the pharmacy.
247 CMR 9.12 requires a licensed health care facility, a valid patient specific prescription or order, compliance with all laws, regulations and policies, and written device procedures.
Under Policy 2019-02 the pharmacy owns the device and contents until dispensed for administration, and keeps the records onsite for not less than 2 years.
Device medications are in manufacturer's sealed, original packaging or repackaged for a single dose or person, and losses are reported under the pharmacy's licensing body requirements.

Retail emergency-kit devices have a broad loader list that includes nurses; daily-dispensing devices are loaded by a pharmacist or a supervised certified technician or intern, with video and machine-specific registration.

Policy 2023-08 stocking needs a facility with an on-site pharmacy and devices at the MCSR address; trainees III-VI verified, other licensed technicians II-VI verified, certified technicians non-PMP Schedule VI without prior verification.

An Automated Pharmacy System dispenses Schedules IV-VI only, in the same building, anchored, on continuous recordable video, without refrigerated or reconstituted products, with consultation available whenever it dispenses and patient choice.
Pharmacy Processing Automation needs technological verification and, if lots are comingled in a cell, a quarantine policy for a recall of any one lot.
All compliance packaging is non-reclosable, opening-evident, with an unalterable label, within container capacity, USP-compliant, and compatible with its components and the other medications.

Multi-drug-single-dose packaging: solid oral forms, 60-day supply ceiling, no Schedule II or III, no as-needed medications, beyond-use date no later than the shortest manufacturer expiration or 60 days.
A returned multi-drug-single-dose package may be repackaged only for the same patient, with nothing returned to inventory and a record naming the pharmacist.
Reusable planners: patient or agent request, no other pharmacy's product, statutory label for each medication; the 60-day and compatibility terms are Board policy.
Oral prescription drugs go in special packaging under 16 CFR 1700.14(a)(10) unless exempt, directed otherwise in the order, or the purchaser requests otherwise.
Special packaging is child-resistant, not childproof, and shall not be reused; Massachusetts sources searched add no separate child-resistance rule.

decision_logic.condition: A device releases medication to nurses or other licensed professionals for patients in a facility.
decision_logic.action: Apply 247 CMR 9.12 and Policy 2019-02: licensed health care facility, patient-specific prescription or order, written procedures, pharmacy ownership until dispensed for administration, the two-year onsite record set, and single dose or person packaging.

decision_logic.condition: The device belongs to a retail pharmacy and serves an emergency medication kit, hospice inpatient acute use, or daily dispensing.
decision_logic.action: Sort by purpose under Policy 2019-02 and apply that purpose's loader list, machine-specific Controlled Substance Registration and DEA determination, and, for daily dispensing, continuous video.

decision_logic.condition: A technician is to stock a facility device.
decision_logic.action: Check the Policy 2023-08 threshold (on-site pharmacy, MCSR address, procedures and training, quality assurance), then match credential to pathway: trainee III-VI verified, licensed technician II-VI verified, certified technician non-PMP Schedule VI without prior verification.

decision_logic.condition: A patient will collect a filled prescription from a machine.
decision_logic.action: Apply 247 CMR 9.10: Schedules IV-VI, same building, anchored, recordable video, no refrigerated or reconstituted products, technological verification, audit trail of recipients, consultation during all dispensing hours, patient choice; add Policy 2022-07's approval request before use.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy's own equipment counts, fills or labels.
decision_logic.action: Apply 247 CMR 9.11: technological verification, and a lot-quarantine procedure if lots are comingled in a cell, plus the listed procedures.

decision_logic.condition: Medications are to go in a compliance package.
decision_logic.action: Name the type, apply every 247 CMR 9.08(1) condition, then the type's own rules: oral liquid one commercial product unless compounded; single-drug solid oral with labeling and bar-code identification if prepared early; multi-drug solid oral with the 60-day, Schedule II or III and as-needed limits.

decision_logic.condition: A patient returns a multi-drug-single-dose package.
decision_logic.action: Accept only a package this pharmacy dispensed, repackage for that same patient, relabel, keep removed medication out of inventory and away from other patients, and record the change with the pharmacist's identity.

decision_logic.condition: A patient or agent asks for a reusable daily dosage planner.
decision_logic.action: Refuse any product another pharmacy dispensed, prepare in the designated space under written procedures, label with the statutory information for each medication, and follow Policy 2023-01's compatibility and 60-day terms.

decision_logic.condition: An oral prescription drug is being dispensed for use at home.
decision_logic.action: Use special packaging unless the drug is listed as exempt in 16 CFR 1700.14(a)(10), the order directs a noncomplying package, or the purchaser requests one; never reuse the special packaging.

decision_logic.condition: The purchaser asks for conventional caps on everything.
decision_logic.action: Rely on the blanket request as CPSC staff guidance allows, preferably recorded in writing, and check it periodically; do not infer a blanket request from a single-prescription request.

ma_vs_federal.text: Child-resistant packaging of dispensed oral prescription drugs is governed by the federal Poison Prevention Packaging Act and 16 CFR part 1700; the Massachusetts sources searched add no separate standard, and 15 U.S.C. 1476 bars a non-identical State standard except as 1476(b) and (c) provide.
Massachusetts compliance packaging conditions in 247 CMR 9.08 and the federal special packaging requirement apply together to the same package; meeting one does not satisfy the other.

Policy 2019-02 requires a machine-specific Controlled Substance Registration for certain retail devices and leaves the pharmacy to determine whether a machine-specific DEA number is required, or requires one if applicable; the federal registration rules themselves are not restated in the policy.

Policy 2022-07 directs a pharmacy storing Schedule IV, V or gabapentin prescriptions in an Automated Pharmacy System to consult the DEA for any additional requirements, alongside Massachusetts PMP reporting.
A Massachusetts rule on controlled substances in these texts reaches Schedule VI prescription drugs, which are not federally controlled.

exceptions.text: Policy 2019-02 applies unless otherwise authorized jointly by the Board and the Drug Control Program.
An ordinary licensed pharmacy technician may load a retail emergency-kit device only for Schedules III through VI.
A pharmacy technician trainee may stock under Policy 2023-08 without direct pharmacist supervision, but still under a pharmacist's direction and supervision and only within the policy's conditions.
The certified technician's no-prior-verification pathway excludes PMP drugs such as gabapentin even though they are Schedule VI.
Comingling lot numbers in a Pharmacy Processing Automation cell is permitted if a quarantine policy for a single-lot recall is maintained.
More than one commercially available medication may go in an oral-liquid-single-dose package when compounded pursuant to a prescription.
A Schedule II or III drug barred from a multi-drug-single-dose package may still be placed in a single-drug-single-dose package if the other conditions are met.
A returned multi-drug-single-dose package may be repackaged and re-dispensed, but only to the same patient.
The listed exemptions in 16 CFR 1700.14(a)(10), such as sublingual nitroglycerin and prednisone tablets in packages of no more than 105 mg, need no special packaging.
A noncomplying package may be used when directed in the prescriber's order or requested by the purchaser.
CPSC staff guidance states that drugs for patients confined in a hospital, or supplied to a traditional nursing home where staff administer doses, need not be in special packaging.

timing_deadlines.event: Retention of automated dispensing device records
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not less than 2 years, onsite at the pharmacy
timing_deadlines.consequence: Records not readily available on request fall short of Policy 2019-02, which 247 CMR 9.12(3) makes part of lawful device use.

timing_deadlines.event: Supply dispensed in a multi-drug-single-dose package
Beyond-use date on each drug in a multi-drug-single-dose package
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not beyond the shortest original manufacturer expiration date or 60 days

timing_deadlines.event: Supply dispensed in a reusable daily dosage planner
timing_deadlines.timeframe: No more than a 60-day supply under Board policy
timing_deadlines.consequence: Departs from Policy 2023-01, which states the limit; 247 CMR 9.07 does not.
Re-dispensing without the 247 CMR 9.08(5) label violates 9.08(4)(a).

timing_deadlines.event: Identifying a single-drug-single-dose package prepared before a prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: Without bar-code scanning or similar technology then, 247 CMR 9.08(2)(b) is not met.

timing_deadlines.event: Pharmacist consultation for Automated Pharmacy System users
timing_deadlines.timeframe: During all hours the system is in operation for dispensing
timing_deadlines.consequence: After-hours dispensing without available consultation fails 247 CMR 9.10(1)(g).

timing_deadlines.event: Written request for Board approval of an Automated Pharmacy System
timing_deadlines.consequence: Operating before the request departs from Policy 2022-07.

forms_records.text: Automated dispensing device records under Policy 2019-02: documentation of licensing-body approval if applicable, locations of all devices, delivery manifests or similar electronic documentation of controlled-substance transport between pharmacy and device, and cleaning and maintenance logs.

Device event data under Policy 2019-02: identity of all personnel who access the contents, location accessed, type of transaction with date and time stamp, name, strength, dosage form and quantity of product, patient name or identifier, and reconciliation of all inventory activities.

247 CMR 9.12(4) device policies and procedures: location, operation and maintenance, security, controlled substances accountability, quality assurance, stocking and return activities, patient confidentiality.

Policy 2023-08 records and procedures: written procedures for the permitted stocking activities including training requirements, and the designated licensee's verification of all transactions, access monitoring, tracking and trending, and random audits.

Automated Pharmacy System: an electronic audit trail including the identity of each person to whom a drug was released, and procedures on location, operation and maintenance, security, controlled substances accountability, quality assurance, stocking and return, and patient confidentiality; Policy 2022-07's approval request lists the system type, hours, schedules, security measures and a completed Application for Pharmacy Modifications.

Pharmacy Processing Automation procedures: operation and maintenance, security, controlled substance accountability, quality assurance, stocking and return, and a lot quarantine procedure when lots are comingled.
Compliance packaging procedures for each type used: cleaning, labeling, dispensing, proper hand hygiene, quarantine and reverse distribution, with drug accountability added by Policy 2023-01.
Multi-drug-single-dose repackaging record: accounts for and documents any repackaging, removal or re-dispensing and identifies the pharmacist making the change.

Compliance package label: statutory and USP information for each medication; name, strength, physical description and total quantity; dispensing or preparation date; multi-drug beyond-use date; pharmacy telephone number; and cell labels with drug name and strength when cells are removable.

Reusable planner: procedures on cleaning, labeling, dispensing and hand hygiene (with container-integrity inspection and drug accountability under Policy 2023-01) and a label with the information required by M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21 for each medication.
Conventional packaging request: no written form is required by the Act or regulations; CPSC staff recommend a written request, particularly for a blanket request.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy using an automated dispensing device
role_duties.duty: Place it only in a licensed health care facility, dispense only on patient-specific authorization, keep the 247 CMR 9.12(4) procedures, own the stock until dispensed for administration, and keep the Policy 2019-02 records onsite for 2 years.

role_duties.role: Health care facility hosting a device
role_duties.duty: If it has no on-site pharmacy, determine whether its licensing body must approve the device's use and placement, and maintain policies, procedures and quality assurance programs for safety, accuracy, security, accountability, confidentiality and proper functioning.

role_duties.role: Retail pharmacy running a daily-dispensing device
role_duties.duty: Obtain the machine-specific Controlled Substance Registration and a machine-specific DEA number if applicable, keep the device on continuous video, and have it loaded only by a pharmacist or a supervised certified technician or intern.
May load a retail pharmacy's emergency-kit or similar approved-use device; is not a listed loader for a daily-dispensing device.
At an eligible facility, load pharmacist-verified Schedule III-VI stock and remove expired Schedule III-VI stock with electronic validation, under a pharmacist's direction and supervision.

role_duties.role: Licensed pharmacy technician other than a trainee
role_duties.duty: At an eligible facility and under pharmacist supervision, load pharmacist-verified Schedule II-VI stock and remove expired Schedule II-VI stock with electronic validation; at a retail emergency-kit device, load Schedules III-VI only.
Without prior pharmacist verification, move non-patient specific, non-PMP Schedule VI stock without further manipulation from an electronic inventory system into a device using electronic validation.
Verify all device transactions against inventory sent or expected back, monitor all access, track and trend data for accuracy and compliance, with random audits in the stocking process.

role_duties.role: Licensed health care professional removing or administering from a device
role_duties.duty: Use bar code scanning or other electronic validation for product verification upon removal and/or upon patient administration.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy operating an Automated Pharmacy System
role_duties.duty: Meet each 247 CMR 9.10(1) condition, keep the 9.10(2) procedures, let patients choose not to use it, provide consultation whenever it dispenses, and submit Policy 2022-07's written approval request before use.
Make the change recorded when a multi-drug-single-dose package is repackaged, and, with the pharmacy, label and bar-code identify single-drug-single-dose packages prepared before a prescription.

Keep within container capacity, one commercial product per oral-liquid-single-dose package unless compounded, no Schedule II or III or as-needed drugs and no more than 60 days in multi-drug-single-dose packages, and label every package under 247 CMR 9.08(5).

role_duties.role: Dispensing pharmacist under the Poison Prevention Packaging Act
role_duties.duty: Put non-exempt oral prescription drugs in special packaging unless the order directs or the purchaser requests otherwise, and do not reuse special packaging; CPSC staff guidance places the retail determination on the dispensing pharmacist.
May direct a noncomplying package in the order for a prescription; on CPSC staff guidance that direction reaches refills of that prescription only.
May request a noncomplying package, including by a blanket request for all prescriptions, and may later ask for special packaging again.

common_traps.text: Applying 247 CMR 9.12's facility and patient-specific conditions to a patient pickup kiosk, or 247 CMR 9.10's Schedule IV-VI limit to a hospital dispensing cabinet.
Saying Policy 2019-02 always requires licensing-body approval; the facility without an on-site pharmacy determines whether approval is required.
Giving the emergency-kit loader list, which includes nurses and ordinary technicians, to a daily-dispensing device.
Using a Policy 2023-08 pathway at a clinic without an on-site pharmacy or at an address not on the facility's MCSR.
Letting a certified technician load gabapentin without prior pharmacist verification because it is Schedule VI.
Stocking refrigerated insulin or a Schedule II prescription in an Automated Pharmacy System.
Treating a pharmacist's visual check as the technological verification 247 CMR 9.11 requires, or treating comingled lots as prohibited.
Turning the Schedule II and III multi-drug-single-dose limit into a ban on all compliance packaging, or finding a maintenance exception in it.
Forgetting the as-needed exclusion and the 60-day supply ceiling for multi-drug-single-dose packages.
Returning tablets removed from a patient's returned multi-drug-single-dose package to stock.
Filling a planner with another pharmacy's product because the bottle is sealed and in date.
Citing 247 CMR 9.07 for the planner's 60-day limit, which is in Policy 2023-01.
Assuming a tamper-evident or non-reclosable compliance package is child-resistant.
Treating a single-prescription request for a snap cap as a blanket request, or a prescriber's direction for one prescription as covering the patient's others.
Presenting CPSC staff guidance, such as the written-request recommendation or the glass-container view, as regulation.
Looking for a Massachusetts child-resistance rule in 247 CMR 9.08; the requirement for dispensed oral prescription drugs is federal.

drug_examples.teaching_point: Schedule VI in Massachusetts but reportable to the PMP, so it is excluded from the certified technician's no-prior-verification stocking pathway while remaining loadable through the verified-stock pathways; Policy 2022-07 also names it for identity collection at kiosk pickup.

A Schedule VI prescription drug not reportable to the PMP, so non-patient specific stock fits the certified technician's no-prior-verification pathway when transferred without manipulation with electronic validation.

Schedule II: outside a trainee's device stocking range and outside an Automated Pharmacy System, and barred from multi-drug-single-dose packages though a single-drug-single-dose package is not barred by that limit.
Schedule III: may not be dispensed in a multi-drug-single-dose package whether or not the patient takes it daily as maintenance therapy.
Schedule IV: within the Automated Pharmacy System schedule range and not excluded from multi-drug-single-dose packaging by schedule, unless taken as needed.
A refrigerated product, so it may not be stocked in an Automated Pharmacy System regardless of its Schedule VI status.
Schedule II: cannot be picked up from an Automated Pharmacy System and cannot go in a multi-drug-single-dose package.
